title: When Do Self-Supervised Representations Help Speech Restoration?

paper.title: When Do Self-Supervised Representations Help Speech Restoration?
paper.abstract: Abstract Self-supervised learning (SSL) representations are widely used in speech restoration (SR), and the prevailing trend is SSL feature cleansing: fine-tuning the SSL to recover clean features from degraded speech, then conditioning the restoration model on them. However, the representational capability of SSL when encoding degraded speech has been underexplored, and we ask whether cleansing always benefits SR training. Across SSL encoders and perceptual quality proxies, we discover perceptual correlation collapse—under severe degradation, cleansing degraded SSL features toward clean ones misaligns with the SR objective. We hypothesize the restoration backbone can supply the SSL with clues to resolve this collapse, since its intermediate layers already produce partially restored features. We therefore propose Early Restoration Injection (ERI), which routes intermediate features from the restoration backbone into the SSL through a lightweight conditioning network. ERI excels over the unconditioned baseline and, on the VoiceFixer benchmark, achieves competitive performance among multiple baselines.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Speech restoration (SR) aims to recover clean speech from degraded speech, where the degradation may be noise, reverberation, bandwidth limitation, clipping. Self-supervised learning (SSL) representations [ 4 , 2 ] have been widely used to address SR for their rich acoustic and phonetic information, and strong alignment with perceptual quality [ 1 ] . One line of research feeds both the SR output and the clean speech into an SSL separately and minimizes the loss between the two resulting representations, utilizing SSL as a guiding signal in training. MaskSR2 [ 16 ] uses HuBERT [ 7 ] as a semantic teacher to conduct knowledge distillation, improving intelligibility. Universe++ [ 29 ] uses an SSL-finetuned phoneme prediction model [ 36 ] to minimize the connectionist temporal classification loss [ 6 ] between the predicted phonemes of the clean and restored speech. In this way, rich SSL representations can be efficiently learned since SSL is only required in the training phase. Another line of research feeds the degraded speech directly to speech SSL and then injects the resulting degraded SSL representation into the SR model as a conditioning feature. Early efforts [ 30 , 3 ] utilize WavLM [ 4 ] as a feature encoder for speech enhancement, paving the way for SSL-conditioned SR. FINALLY [ 1 ] uses WavLM features as conditioning signals to jointly perform speech enhancement and bandwidth extension. These methods directly integrate SSL models into the enhancement model’s forward path, effectively leveraging the rich representational power of SSLs. Beyond using SSL representations as a mere guiding signal in training or as conditioning features, recent approaches first restore the SSL features, then use cleansed features as conditions for SR models. This so-called SSL feature cleansing recovers clean SSL features given a degraded speech waveform either by using language models (LM) or by fine-tuning SSL itself. GenSE [ 39 ] and SenSE [ 14 ] are two representative methods that use LM to generate the recovered SSL features given noisy SSL features. Miipher [ 12 ] , SIDON [ 19 ] , PASE [ 27 ] , and StuPASE [ 26 ] incorporate pretraining where SSL models are fine-tuned to restore the clean SSL features by themselves. LM-based SSL feature cleansing requires demanding computational resources, while fine-tuning-based SSL feature cleansing is relatively less compute- and memory-intensive. Though fine-tuning SSL for feature cleansing has proven effective for SR tasks, existing approaches have mainly depended on empirical results to show these performance gains. SSL feature distance has been studied as a property of the representation — how a layer’s clean–degraded distance relates to its importance for speech enhancement [ 9 ] . Feature cleansing, by contrast, minimizes this distance, and in doing so presupposes that a smaller distance implies better restored speech — an assumption that has not been examined. We pose a fundamental question: is SSL feature cleansing always effective for SR? Across multiple SSL encoders and perceptual quality proxies, we find perceptual correlation collapse : the correlation between SSL feature distance and perceptual quality holds under mild degradation but breaks past a critical severity, so that minimizing the SSL loss no longer tracks quality beyond this point. One simple solution to this phenomenon is to place a preliminary restoration model before the SSL so that the SSL never sees severely degraded speech and instead consumes the decoded waveform that model produces; this buys clean-enough input, but at the cost of an auxiliary model. In fact, the SR backbone we already have produces partially restored features at its intermediate layers. This leads to our central hypothesis: if those features are already restored enough to serve as evidence, exposing them to the SSL should mitigate perceptual correlation collapse, obtaining the benefit of pre-restoration without a separate pre-restoration model. To validate this, we propose Early Restoration Injection (ERI) , a method that injects intermediate layer SR features into the SSL via a simple conditioning network. This method effectively resolves the perceptual correlation collapse by feeding SSL with partially recovered speech features, converging to higher quality than the unconditioned baseline at a matched parameter count. Our contributions are two-fold: • We discover perceptual correlation collapse : as degradation increases, cleansing degraded SSL features does not fully track perceptual quality. We establish this with analysis across multiple SSL models and perceptual-quality proxies. • We propose Early Restoration Injection (ERI) , a simple yet novel method that injects intermediate features from the SR network into SSL feature cleansing. Our framework achieves competitive performance on the VoiceFixer benchmark. Figure 1 : t-SNE plots of speech degraded with additive noise at varying SNR level, visualized in WavLM feature space. sections.heading: 2 When do self-supervised representations help speech restoration?
sections.text: We first show how SSL represents degraded speech, using a motivating visualization in which some SSL features lose the speech identity and become indistinguishable from those of noise even when the speech is audible. Then we discover perceptual correlation collapse , a phenomenon where SSL feature cleansing does not correspond to perceptual quality increase if speech degradation is severe.

sections.heading: 2.1 Some utterances lose their identity in the SSL feature space at low SNRs, while others remain firmly anchored to their clean counterparts.
sections.text: Method We design a toy visualization using t-SNE [ 32 ] . We sample m m speech utterances from FLEURS-R [ 17 ] and LibriTTS-R [ 11 ] and m m noise samples from WHAM! [ 34 ] and DNS Challenge 2020 [ 23 ] , thus formulating a pair ( x j , n j ) (x_{j},n_{j}) , where x x , n n , and j j represent speech data, noise data, and the data index, respectively. For each pair, we synthesize noisy copies at SNR ranging from − 20 -20 to 20 20 dB in 2 2 dB increments. Together with the clean speech and the noise data, each data pair of index j j yields 23 conditions. The samples are then fed individually to the SSL, and the resulting feature representations are visualized using t-SNE. We used the final-layer feature (time frame-pooled) of WavLM [ 4 ] for the visualization. We set m m to 25. Finding Fig. 1 shows t-SNE embeddings of WavLM features for a set of utterances, each mixed with its own noise sample across several SNR levels; the utterance index j j is marked at each point, with clean speech in bold black and noise in pink. Since SNR is the only source of variation within an utterance, a representation encoding speech content should organize by index, with degraded samples remaining near their clean anchor. Region (i) behaves this way: samples sharing an index stay together, and SNR governs how far each sits from its anchor. Region (ii) does not. Degraded samples do not simply disperse; they converge onto the region occupied by the noise embeddings, despite each utterance carrying a different noise sample. Most importantly, they do not arrive together: some noisy samples reach region (ii) at around 0 0 dB (See j = 11 , 16 , 19 j=11,16,19 ), where speech and noise carry similar power, while others at the same SNR stay beside their anchors. We can see that some utterances lose their speech features even when the speech is audible.

sections.heading: 2.2 Lower SSL loss does not always translate into higher perceptual quality, especially when speech degradation is severe.
sections.text: From the t-SNE visualization, we observe that some utterances lose their utterance identity in SSL feature space when they are not supposed to (e.g., 0 dB; even when the speech is audible). Thus, we conjecture that in multi-degradation scenarios, the SSL feature distance would not reflect the true perceptual quality if the degradation severity is beyond a certain level. However, a single degradation configuration (e.g., SNR) cannot represent the overall perceptual quality in a multi-degradation scenario, motivating us to use perceptual quality evaluation metrics as proxies for thorough analysis. Method We randomly sample m m clean English utterances x 1 x_{1} , x 2 x_{2} , … \ldots , x m x_{m} from LibriTTS-R [ 11 ] . For each clean utterance x j x_{j} where j = 1 , … , m j=1,...,m , four degraded versions y j ( E ) , y j ( M ) , y j ( D ) , y j ( X ) y_{j}^{(E)},y_{j}^{(M)},y_{j}^{(D)},y_{j}^{(X)} , corresponding to Easy ( E E ), Moderate ( M M ), Difficult ( D D ), and Extreme ( X X ), respectively, are simulated. The degradation type and the application probability are homogeneous across different degradation severities. The degradation pipeline uses noise, bandwidth limitation, clipping, reverb, and packet loss. Each degradation is sampled from a severity-specific range, chosen to be harsher at every step from Easy to Extreme. Noise SNR drops from [ 12.5 , 20 ] [12.5,20] to [ − 10 , − 2.5 ] [-10,-2.5] dB, the bandwidth cutoff from [ 5750 , 7000 ] [5750,7000] to [ 2000 , 3250 ] [2000,3250] Hz, clipping thresholds tighten inward from [ 0.00 , 0.02 ] / [ 0.98 , 1.00 ] [0.00,0.02]/[0.98,1.00] to [ 0.06 , 0.08 ] / [ 0.92 , 0.94 ] [0.06,0.08]/[0.92,0.94] , and packet loss duration grows from 5 to 20 ms. For each degradation severity, we compute the cosine distance d j ( E ) , d j ( M ) , d j ( D ) , d j ( X ) d_{j}^{(E)},d_{j}^{(M)},d_{j}^{(D)},d_{j}^{(X)} between the SSL output features for clean and degraded speech. The perceptual quality prediction of the degraded speech q j ( E ) , q j ( M ) , q j ( D ) , q j ( X ) q_{j}^{(E)},q_{j}^{(M)},q_{j}^{(D)},q_{j}^{(X)} is computed. For a general analysis, we select multiple SSLs and quality prediction models. For SSL, we use WavLM [ 4 ] , HuBERT [ 7 ] , SPEAR [ 38 ] , and Wav2Vec 2.0 [ 2 ] , all in large variants. For neural quality prediction, we use VQScore [ 5 ] , SCOREQ [ 22 ] , and DNSMOS [ 24 ] . We use the no-reference (NR) version of SCOREQ. Finally, we use log spectral distance (LSD) for model-free quality estimation. To quantify the correlation between the SSL distance and quality score, we compute the Spearman correlation ρ ( sev ) \rho^{(\mathrm{sev})} [ 31 ] over the m m paired observations { ( d j , q j ) } j = 1 m \{(d_{j},q_{j})\}^{m}_{j=1} , for each severity. sev \mathrm{sev} represents degradation severity index, and the correlation coefficient represents Perceptual correlation of SSL loss. For robust analysis, we set m m to 100, and conduct bootstrapping for 1,000 times and plot both the mean correlation and standard deviation. The SSL output feature is computed as the time frame-wise mean of the final layer output. Finding Fig. 2 shows that the perceptual correlation (SSL-loss/quality correlation) is strong under mild degradation but collapses beyond a critical severity, implying SSL feature distance between clean and severely degraded speech does not rank-order perceptual quality well. This has a consequence for SSL feature cleansing: minimizing SSL loss does not always translate into higher perceptual quality when the speech degradation is severe. We verify that this collapse is not an artifact of any single design choice in the analysis. First, it is not specific to a particular SSL model: the same trend appears across all four representations, indicating that the collapse reflects a property of the SSL loss-quality relationship rather than a trait of one SSL feature space. Second, to rule out sampling noise as the cause, we bootstrap each correlation estimate and report the resulting standard deviation in Fig. 2 ; the collapse persists well outside this uncertainty band, confirming that it is a stable trend rather than a sampling artifact. Third, to check whether the collapse is instead an artifact of the perceptual quality metric itself, we repeat the analysis with LSD, a model-free quality estimator computed directly from the log-spectral distance. Although LSD may not perfectly track subjective perceptual quality, it exhibits the same collapse beyond the critical severity, which suggests the effect is a genuine property of the SSL representation rather than an artifact of the particular quality metric used to measure it. Together, these results expose a critical problem for SSL-conditioned SR. An SSL distance objective provides less useful gradient toward perceptual quality in the severe regime that restoration must handle. We therefore explain our proposed method to provide the SSL encoder with restored features in the next section.

sections.heading: 3 Early Restoration Injection
sections.text: Fig. 3 shows the overall framework of ERI. SEMamba++ [ 13 ] and WavLM [ 4 ] are used as the SR and speech SSL models, respectively. SEMamba++ comprises an encoder, bottleneck, and decoder. The encoder encodes the degraded speech into hidden features. The bottleneck is a 4-layer sequence of time-frequency processing modules. The decoder maps the restored features into the magnitude and phase spectrogram, converting to the clean waveform. WavLM comprises a feature extractor followed by 24 transformer layers. ERI is a simple method to feed the SSL with the latent bottleneck feature of SEMamba++. The latent bottleneck feature has a shape of T , F , D T,F,D , where T T , F F , and D D represent the time, frequency, and channel dimensions of SEMamba++. ERI first reshapes the latent bottleneck feature to T , F ​ D T,FD , followed by a linear layer that maps the dimension F ​ D FD to C C , where C C represents the channel dimension of WavLM. After applying Layer normalization and LeakyReLU activation, we apply adaptive average pooling to match the time dimension to T ′ T^{\prime} , corresponding to the time dimension of WavLM. The resulting feature is concatenated with the WavLM feature of shape T ′ , C T^{\prime},C after the convolutional feature extractor, deriving the feature of shape T ′ , 2 ​ C T^{\prime},2C . Then a linear layer maps the feature into T ′ , C T^{\prime},C so that the condition injection is made. Figure 3 : Model architecture and training framework. WavLM is fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 8 ] , where the hyperparameters r r and α \alpha were set to 16 and 32, respectively. After WavLM takes the degraded waveform and the ERI condition to restore the SSL feature, the restored SSL feature is injected back into the SR backbone via the SSL condition fusion module. The SSL condition fusion module is an adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) [ 35 ] -based module fusing the SSL condition into SEMamba++. We use the layer 24 output from WavLM to conduct SSL condition fusion, as done by previous work [ 27 ] . We extract the ERI condition from SEMamba++ layer 2 and fuse the cleansed SSL features back at layer 3. We apply stop-gradient (sg) before ERI and SSL condition fusion. sg before ERI blocks the SSL loss from reaching SEMamba++. In particular, this prevents the SSL loss from acting as a representation alignment [ 40 ] loss: SEMamba++ is trained only by the SR objective, so any effect of ERI is gained via the forward path rather than by SSL gradients shaping SEMamba++. sg before SSL condition fusion prevents the spectrogram-level SR loss from reaching WavLM, keeping it focused on the SSL feature cleansing. We found empirically that without sg before SSL condition fusion, the SSL loss was not effectively minimized and performance degraded.

sections.heading: 3.1 Training objective
sections.text: The training objective can be divided into learning SR and SSL models. For training the SR model, we followed the LSGAN [ 18 ] configuration from SEMamba++. For training the SSL feature cleansing, we utilized an L2-normalized MSE loss of the 24th-layer features ℒ SSL \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SSL}} . We append ℒ SSL \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SSL}} to the generator loss so that the training can be conducted end-to-end, simultaneously optimizing both the SR and SSL models. The final generator loss is ℒ total = ℒ G + ℒ SSL \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{G}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SSL}} .

sections.heading: 4.1 Training
sections.text: Datasets For speech, we used VCTK-0.92 [ 37 ] and LibriTTS-R [ 11 ] . For VCTK, we excluded speakers in p280 and p315 following [ 15 ] . For LibriTTS-R, we used the train-clean-100 and -360 subsets, totaling 300 hours of speech sources. For noise data, we used WHAM! [ 34 ] and DNS challenge [ 23 ] . For RIR, we used Arni [ 21 ] and the DNS challenge [ 23 ] . All data were sampled at 16 kHz and split into a train and a testset, including the noise and RIR data. Note that LibriTTS-R already has a predetermined testset. Degradation simulation Noise, reverberation, bandwidth limitation, and clipping were used to simulate degradation. In training, various distortions are randomly applied with predetermined probabilities. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) ranged from -5 to 20 dB, and bandwidth reduction was applied at various cutoff frequencies (2-7 kHz). For clipping, we followed the official configurations [ 42 ] . Training configurations The segment size of 48,000 samples (3 seconds) was used for training. For STFT, we used a Hann window with a window length of 400 samples and a hop size of 160 samples. We set the learning rate to 1e-4 and used the AdamW optimizer with β 1 \beta_{1} and β 2 \beta_{2} set to 0.8 and 0.99, respectively. We set the batch size to 8 and used exponential learning rate decay with γ = 0.99 \gamma=0.99 . ERI was trained in two stages. In stage 1, SEMamba++ was trained with the same data configuration. In stage 2, we trained the full ERI framework for an additional 300k steps.

sections.heading: 4.2 Evaluation
sections.text: Datasets For comparisons within our model, we used a simulated set built from the test split in Section 4.1 . For system comparison against other methods, we used the official VoiceFixer test set [ 15 ] , which covers noise, reverb, bandwidth limitation, and clipping. Baseline methods For GAN methods, we used VoiceFixer [ 15 ] and SEMamba++ [ 13 ] . For generative methods, we used AnyEnhance [ 41 ] . For SSL-based methods, we used SIDON [ 19 ] . sections.heading: 5 Experimental results
sections.text: Table 1 illustrates the results of multiple baseline models evaluated on the VoiceFixer testset for benchmarking SR. ERI attains the best PESQ, ESTOI, and LPS, indicating strong signal fidelity and intelligibility in the restored speech, while its second-best UTMOS keeps perceptual quality competitive. Although ERI substantially increases the parameter count due to the added SSL and conditioning modules, its real-time factor (measured on a single RTX 4090 GPU) increases only from 0.015 for SEMamba++ to 0.020 for ERI, showing that the inference efficiency is not heavily compromised. Table 2 measures the effectiveness of ERI (✓) compared to the baseline (✗). The baseline minimizes SSL loss without ERI features. To compensate for the parameter increase in ERI, we double the hyperparameters r r and α \alpha and attach LoRA to both feed-forward networks (FFNs) rather than the second FFN alone (i.e., default design), resulting in a parameter gap of less than 1M. ERI improves performance over the baseline, showing the effectiveness of intermediate features from the SR backbone for SSL feature cleansing. Moreover, since ERI feeds restored intermediate features of the SR backbone, the effectiveness of ERI could be compromised if the SR backbone is not fully converged. To test this, we instantiate ERI with the SR backbone trained less in Stage 1 (i.e., 300k steps). As shown in Table 2 , ERI remains effective even with such a setup, showing that ERI does not require full convergence of the SR backbone for its success. Lastly, to show that our method could be applied to other SSLs analyzed in Section 2 , we design an ERI variant where the SSL is HuBERT. Fig. 4 shows that ERI enables effective translation of SSL loss minimization into perceptual quality gain. Using SCOREQ and SSL loss values after initial training stabilization as anchors, we define Perceptual gain ratio as the SCOREQ increment per 10 − 3 10^{-3} reduction in SSL loss. The ratio substantially favors ERI, implying that SSL loss minimization more effectively leads to perceptual quality gain when equipped with ERI. Note that analyzing the perceptual correlation from Section 2.2 on a fully trained ERI is confounded, as at convergence both w/ ERI and w/o ERI learn to cleanse SSL features. The perceptual gain ratio instead directly measures whether ERI translates the SSL objective to perceptual quality in training. Design study Table 3 shows the design choice study results to measure the component-wise contribution in the proposed method. Modifying the ERI layer from 2 to 1 degrades perceptual quality, suggesting that injecting more restored features into the SSL backbone improves performance. Removing the sg on the SSL condition fusion degrades perceptual quality, attributable to the ineffective SSL loss minimization discussed in Section 3 . Lastly, changing the ERI mechanism from simple concatenation (i.e., default design) to more complicated AdaLN did not result in a significant performance gain, implying that ERI’s benefit comes from the intermediate-layer features themselves rather than the increased capacity.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusions
sections.text: We discover perceptual correlation collapse: under severe degradation, the SSL feature cleansing objective does not fully align with the restoration objective. Though our correlation analysis relies on neural quality proxies for human perception, the agreement we observe across multiple proxies shows the trend is not an artifact of a single metric. To address perceptual correlation collapse, we propose Early Restoration Injection (ERI), which conditions SSL feature cleansing on intermediate features from the restoration model, supplying the SSL with partially restored evidence in place of severely degraded input. ERI adds only simple operations, and our experiments attribute its gain to the injected features themselves rather than to added capacity or a more expressive fusion mechanism. ERI improves over the unconditioned baseline at matched parameter count, and performs competitively against multiple baseline models.

Yongjoon Lee Younghoo Kwon Jung-Woo Choi † † thanks: * Corresponding author. Abstract Self-supervised learning (SSL) representations are widely used in speech restoration (SR), and the prevailing trend is SSL feature cleansing: fine-tuning the SSL to recover clean features from degraded speech, then conditioning the restoration model on them. However, the representational capability of SSL when encoding degraded speech has been underexplored, and we ask whether cleansing always benefits SR training. Across SSL encoders and perceptual quality proxies, we discover perceptual correlation collapse—under severe degradation, cleansing degraded SSL features toward clean ones misaligns with the SR objective. We hypothesize the restoration backbone can supply the SSL with clues to resolve this collapse, since its intermediate layers already produce partially restored features. We therefore propose Early Restoration Injection (ERI), which routes intermediate features from the restoration backbone into the SSL through a lightweight conditioning network. ERI excels over the unconditioned baseline and, on the VoiceFixer benchmark, achieves competitive performance among multiple baselines. Index Terms: Speech restoration, Self-supervised learning † † address: 1 School of Electrical Engineering, KAIST, Daejeon, South Korea 2 Department of AI Systems, KAIST, Daejeon, South Korea 1 Introduction Speech restoration (SR) aims to recover clean speech from degraded speech, where the degradation may be noise, reverberation, bandwidth limitation, clipping. Self-supervised learning (SSL) representations [ 4 , 2 ] have been widely used to address SR for their rich acoustic and phonetic information, and strong alignment with perceptual quality [ 1 ] . One line of research feeds both the SR output and the clean speech into an SSL separately and minimizes the loss between the two resulting representations, utilizing SSL as a guiding signal in training. MaskSR2 [ 16 ] uses HuBERT [ 7 ] as a semantic teacher to conduct knowledge distillation, improving intelligibility. Universe++ [ 29 ] uses an SSL-finetuned phoneme prediction model [ 36 ] to minimize the connectionist temporal classification loss [ 6 ] between the predicted phonemes of the clean and restored speech. In this way, rich SSL representations can be efficiently learned since SSL is only required in the training phase. Another line of research feeds the degraded speech directly to speech SSL and then injects the resulting degraded SSL representation into the SR model as a conditioning feature. Early efforts [ 30 , 3 ] utilize WavLM [ 4 ] as a feature encoder for speech enhancement, paving the way for SSL-conditioned SR. FINALLY [ 1 ] uses WavLM features as conditioning signals to jointly perform speech enhancement and bandwidth extension. These methods directly integrate SSL models into the enhancement model’s forward path, effectively leveraging the rich representational power of SSLs. Beyond using SSL representations as a mere guiding signal in training or as conditioning features, recent approaches first restore the SSL features, then use cleansed features as conditions for SR models. This so-called SSL feature cleansing recovers clean SSL features given a degraded speech waveform either by using language models (LM) or by fine-tuning SSL itself. GenSE [ 39 ] and SenSE [ 14 ] are two representative methods that use LM to generate the recovered SSL features given noisy SSL features. Miipher [ 12 ] , SIDON [ 19 ] , PASE [ 27 ] , and StuPASE [ 26 ] incorporate pretraining where SSL models are fine-tuned to restore the clean SSL features by themselves. LM-based SSL feature cleansing requires demanding computational resources, while fine-tuning-based SSL feature cleansing is relatively less compute- and memory-intensive. Though fine-tuning SSL for feature cleansing has proven effective for SR tasks, existing approaches have mainly depended on empirical results to show these performance gains. SSL feature distance has been studied as a property of the representation — how a layer’s clean–degraded distance relates to its importance for speech enhancement [ 9 ] . Feature cleansing, by contrast, minimizes this distance, and in doing so presupposes that a smaller distance implies better restored speech — an assumption that has not been examined. We pose a fundamental question: is SSL feature cleansing always effective for SR? Across multiple SSL encoders and perceptual quality proxies, we find perceptual correlation collapse : the correlation between SSL feature distance and perceptual quality holds under mild degradation but breaks past a critical severity, so that minimizing the SSL loss no longer tracks quality beyond this point. One simple solution to this phenomenon is to place a preliminary restoration model before the SSL so that the SSL never sees severely degraded speech and instead consumes the decoded waveform that model produces; this buys clean-enough input, but at the cost of an auxiliary model. In fact, the SR backbone we already have produces partially restored features at its intermediate layers. This leads to our central hypothesis: if those features are already restored enough to serve as evidence, exposing them to the SSL should mitigate perceptual correlation collapse, obtaining the benefit of pre-restoration without a separate pre-restoration model. To validate this, we propose Early Restoration Injection (ERI) , a method that injects intermediate layer SR features into the SSL via a simple conditioning network. This method effectively resolves the perceptual correlation collapse by feeding SSL with partially recovered speech features, converging to higher quality than the unconditioned baseline at a matched parameter count. Our contributions are two-fold: • We discover perceptual correlation collapse : as degradation increases, cleansing degraded SSL features does not fully track perceptual quality. We establish this with analysis across multiple SSL models and perceptual-quality proxies. • We propose Early Restoration Injection (ERI) , a simple yet novel method that injects intermediate features from the SR network into SSL feature cleansing. Our framework achieves competitive performance on the VoiceFixer benchmark. Figure 1 : t-SNE plots of speech degraded with additive noise at varying SNR level, visualized in WavLM feature space. (a) WavLM (Left) and HuBERT (Right) (b) SPEAR (Left) and Wav2Vec2 (Right) Figure 2 : SSL-wise plot of perceptual correlation. 2 When do self-supervised representations help speech restoration? We first show how SSL represents degraded speech, using a motivating visualization in which some SSL features lose the speech identity and become indistinguishable from those of noise even when the speech is audible. Then we discover perceptual correlation collapse , a phenomenon where SSL feature cleansing does not correspond to perceptual quality increase if speech degradation is severe. 2.1 Some utterances lose their identity in the SSL feature space at low SNRs, while others remain firmly anchored to their clean counterparts. Method We design a toy visualization using t-SNE [ 32 ] . We sample m m speech utterances from FLEURS-R [ 17 ] and LibriTTS-R [ 11 ] and m m noise samples from WHAM! [ 34 ] and DNS Challenge 2020 [ 23 ] , thus formulating a pair ( x j , n j ) (x_{j},n_{j}) , where x x , n n , and j j represent speech data, noise data, and the data index, respectively. For each pair, we synthesize noisy copies at SNR ranging from − 20 -20 to 20 20 dB in 2 2 dB increments. Together with the clean speech and the noise data, each data pair of index j j yields 23 conditions. The samples are then fed individually to the SSL, and the resulting feature representations are visualized using t-SNE. We used the final-layer feature (time frame-pooled) of WavLM [ 4 ] for the visualization. We set m m to 25. Finding Fig. 1 shows t-SNE embeddings of WavLM features for a set of utterances, each mixed with its own noise sample across several SNR levels; the utterance index j j is marked at each point, with clean speech in bold black and noise in pink. Since SNR is the only source of variation within an utterance, a representation encoding speech content should organize by index, with degraded samples remaining near their clean anchor. Region (i) behaves this way: samples sharing an index stay together, and SNR governs how far each sits from its anchor. Region (ii) does not. Degraded samples do not simply disperse; they converge onto the region occupied by the noise embeddings, despite each utterance carrying a different noise sample. Most importantly, they do not arrive together: some noisy samples reach region (ii) at around 0 0 dB (See j = 11 , 16 , 19 j=11,16,19 ), where speech and noise carry similar power, while others at the same SNR stay beside their anchors. We can see that some utterances lose their speech features even when the speech is audible. 2.2 Lower SSL loss does not always translate into higher perceptual quality, especially when speech degradation is severe. From the t-SNE visualization, we observe that some utterances lose their utterance identity in SSL feature space when they are not supposed to (e.g., 0 dB; even when the speech is audible). Thus, we conjecture that in multi-degradation scenarios, the SSL feature distance would not reflect the true perceptual quality if the degradation severity is beyond a certain level. However, a single degradation configuration (e.g., SNR) cannot represent the overall perceptual quality in a multi-degradation scenario, motivating us to use perceptual quality evaluation metrics as proxies for thorough analysis. Method We randomly sample m m clean English utterances x 1 x_{1} , x 2 x_{2} , … \ldots , x m x_{m} from LibriTTS-R [ 11 ] . For each clean utterance x j x_{j} where j = 1 , … , m j=1,...,m , four degraded versions y j ( E ) , y j ( M ) , y j ( D ) , y j ( X ) y_{j}^{(E)},y_{j}^{(M)},y_{j}^{(D)},y_{j}^{(X)} , corresponding to Easy ( E E ), Moderate ( M M ), Difficult ( D D ), and Extreme ( X X ), respectively, are simulated. The degradation type and the application probability are homogeneous across different degradation severities. The degradation pipeline uses noise, bandwidth limitation, clipping, reverb, and packet loss. Each degradation is sampled from a severity-specific range, chosen to be harsher at every step from Easy to Extreme. Noise SNR drops from [ 12.5 , 20 ] [12.5,20] to [ − 10 , − 2.5 ] [-10,-2.5] dB, the bandwidth cutoff from [ 5750 , 7000 ] [5750,7000] to [ 2000 , 3250 ] [2000,3250] Hz, clipping thresholds tighten inward from [ 0.00 , 0.02 ] / [ 0.98 , 1.00 ] [0.00,0.02]/[0.98,1.00] to [ 0.06 , 0.08 ] / [ 0.92 , 0.94 ] [0.06,0.08]/[0.92,0.94] , and packet loss duration grows from 5 to 20 ms. For each degradation severity, we compute the cosine distance d j ( E ) , d j ( M ) , d j ( D ) , d j ( X ) d_{j}^{(E)},d_{j}^{(M)},d_{j}^{(D)},d_{j}^{(X)} between the SSL output features for clean and degraded speech. The perceptual quality prediction of the degraded speech q j ( E ) , q j ( M ) , q j ( D ) , q j ( X ) q_{j}^{(E)},q_{j}^{(M)},q_{j}^{(D)},q_{j}^{(X)} is computed. For a general analysis, we select multiple SSLs and quality prediction models. For SSL, we use WavLM [ 4 ] , HuBERT [ 7 ] , SPEAR [ 38 ] , and Wav2Vec 2.0 [ 2 ] , all in large variants. For neural quality prediction, we use VQScore [ 5 ] , SCOREQ [ 22 ] , and DNSMOS [ 24 ] . We use the no-reference (NR) version of SCOREQ. Finally, we use log spectral distance (LSD) for model-free quality estimation. To quantify the correlation between the SSL distance and quality score, we compute the Spearman correlation ρ ( sev ) \rho^{(\mathrm{sev})} [ 31 ] over the m m paired observations { ( d j , q j ) } j = 1 m \{(d_{j},q_{j})\}^{m}_{j=1} , for each severity. sev \mathrm{sev} represents degradation severity index, and the correlation coefficient represents Perceptual correlation of SSL loss. For robust analysis, we set m m to 100, and conduct bootstrapping for 1,000 times and plot both the mean correlation and standard deviation. The SSL output feature is computed as the time frame-wise mean of the final layer output. Finding Fig. 2 shows that the perceptual correlation (SSL-loss/quality correlation) is strong under mild degradation but collapses beyond a critical severity, implying SSL feature distance between clean and severely degraded speech does not rank-order perceptual quality well. This has a consequence for SSL feature cleansing: minimizing SSL loss does not always translate into higher perceptual quality when the speech degradation is severe. We verify that this collapse is not an artifact of any single design choice in the analysis. First, it is not specific to a particular SSL model: the same trend appears across all four representations, indicating that the collapse reflects a property of the SSL loss-quality relationship rather than a trait of one SSL feature space. Second, to rule out sampling noise as the cause, we bootstrap each correlation estimate and report the resulting standard deviation in Fig. 2 ; the collapse persists well outside this uncertainty band, confirming that it is a stable trend rather than a sampling artifact. Third, to check whether the collapse is instead an artifact of the perceptual quality metric itself, we repeat the analysis with LSD, a model-free quality estimator computed directly from the log-spectral distance. Although LSD may not perfectly track subjective perceptual quality, it exhibits the same collapse beyond the critical severity, which suggests the effect is a genuine property of the SSL representation rather than an artifact of the particular quality metric used to measure it. Together, these results expose a critical problem for SSL-conditioned SR. An SSL distance objective provides less useful gradient toward perceptual quality in the severe regime that restoration must handle. We therefore explain our proposed method to provide the SSL encoder with restored features in the next section. 3 Early Restoration Injection Fig. 3 shows the overall framework of ERI. SEMamba++ [ 13 ] and WavLM [ 4 ] are used as the SR and speech SSL models, respectively. SEMamba++ comprises an encoder, bottleneck, and decoder. The encoder encodes the degraded speech into hidden features. The bottleneck is a 4-layer sequence of time-frequency processing modules. The decoder maps the restored features into the magnitude and phase spectrogram, converting to the clean waveform. WavLM comprises a feature extractor followed by 24 transformer layers. ERI is a simple method to feed the SSL with the latent bottleneck feature of SEMamba++. The latent bottleneck feature has a shape of T , F , D T,F,D , where T T , F F , and D D represent the time, frequency, and channel dimensions of SEMamba++. ERI first reshapes the latent bottleneck feature to T , F ​ D T,FD , followed by a linear layer that maps the dimension F ​ D FD to C C , where C C represents the channel dimension of WavLM. After applying Layer normalization and LeakyReLU activation, we apply adaptive average pooling to match the time dimension to T ′ T^{\prime} , corresponding to the time dimension of WavLM. The resulting feature is concatenated with the WavLM feature of shape T ′ , C T^{\prime},C after the convolutional feature extractor, deriving the feature of shape T ′ , 2 ​ C T^{\prime},2C . Then a linear layer maps the feature into T ′ , C T^{\prime},C so that the condition injection is made. Figure 3 : Model architecture and training framework. WavLM is fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 8 ] , where the hyperparameters r r and α \alpha were set to 16 and 32, respectively. After WavLM takes the degraded waveform and the ERI condition to restore the SSL feature, the restored SSL feature is injected back into the SR backbone via the SSL condition fusion module. The SSL condition fusion module is an adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) [ 35 ] -based module fusing the SSL condition into SEMamba++. We use the layer 24 output from WavLM to conduct SSL condition fusion, as done by previous work [ 27 ] . We extract the ERI condition from SEMamba++ layer 2 and fuse the cleansed SSL features back at layer 3. We apply stop-gradient (sg) before ERI and SSL condition fusion. sg before ERI blocks the SSL loss from reaching SEMamba++. In particular, this prevents the SSL loss from acting as a representation alignment [ 40 ] loss: SEMamba++ is trained only by the SR objective, so any effect of ERI is gained via the forward path rather than by SSL gradients shaping SEMamba++. sg before SSL condition fusion prevents the spectrogram-level SR loss from reaching WavLM, keeping it focused on the SSL feature cleansing. We found empirically that without sg before SSL condition fusion, the SSL loss was not effectively minimized and performance degraded. 3.1 Training objective The training objective can be divided into learning SR and SSL models. For training the SR model, we followed the LSGAN [ 18 ] configuration from SEMamba++. For training the SSL feature cleansing, we utilized an L2-normalized MSE loss of the 24th-layer features ℒ SSL \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SSL}} . We append ℒ SSL \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SSL}} to the generator loss so that the training can be conducted end-to-end, simultaneously optimizing both the SR and SSL models. The final generator loss is ℒ total = ℒ G + ℒ SSL \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{G}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SSL}} . 4 Experimental settings 4.1 Training Datasets For speech, we used VCTK-0.92 [ 37 ] and LibriTTS-R [ 11 ] . For VCTK, we excluded speakers in p280 and p315 following [ 15 ] . For LibriTTS-R, we used the train-clean-100 and -360 subsets, totaling 300 hours of speech sources. For noise data, we used WHAM! [ 34 ] and DNS challenge [ 23 ] . For RIR, we used Arni [ 21 ] and the DNS challenge [ 23 ] . All data were sampled at 16 kHz and split into a train and a testset, including the noise and RIR data. Note that LibriTTS-R already has a predetermined testset. Degradation simulation Noise, reverberation, bandwidth limitation, and clipping were used to simulate degradation. In training, various distortions are randomly applied with predetermined probabilities. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) ranged from -5 to 20 dB, and bandwidth reduction was applied at various cutoff frequencies (2-7 kHz). For clipping, we followed the official configurations [ 42 ] . Training configurations The segment size of 48,000 samples (3 seconds) was used for training. For STFT, we used a Hann window with a window length of 400 samples and a hop size of 160 samples. We set the learning rate to 1e-4 and used the AdamW optimizer with β 1 \beta_{1} and β 2 \beta_{2} set to 0.8 and 0.99, respectively. We set the batch size to 8 and used exponential learning rate decay with γ = 0.99 \gamma=0.99 . ERI was trained in two stages. In stage 1, SEMamba++ was trained with the same data configuration. In stage 2, we trained the full ERI framework for an additional 300k steps. 4.2 Evaluation Datasets For comparisons within our model, we used a simulated set built from the test split in Section 4.1 . For system comparison against other methods, we used the official VoiceFixer test set [ 15 ] , which covers noise, reverb, bandwidth limitation, and clipping. Baseline methods For GAN methods, we used VoiceFixer [ 15 ] and SEMamba++ [ 13 ] . For generative methods, we used AnyEnhance [ 41 ] . For SSL-based methods, we used SIDON [ 19 ] . Lastly, for regressive methods, we used TF-GridNet [ 33 ] . For all models, we used the official checkpoint. Table 1 : Performance evaluation on the VoiceFixer testset. ERI attains the best PESQ, ESTOI, and LPS, indicating strong signal fidelity and intelligibility in the restored speech, while its second-best UTMOS keeps perceptual quality competitive. Although ERI substantially increases the parameter count due to the added SSL and conditioning modules, its real-time factor (measured on a single RTX 4090 GPU) increases only from 0.015 for SEMamba++ to 0.020 for ERI, showing that the inference efficiency is not heavily compromised. To compensate for the parameter increase in ERI, we double the hyperparameters r r and α \alpha and attach LoRA to both feed-forward networks (FFNs) rather than the second FFN alone (i.e., default design), resulting in a parameter gap of less than 1M. Fig. 4 shows that ERI enables effective translation of SSL loss minimization into perceptual quality gain. Using SCOREQ and SSL loss values after initial training stabilization as anchors, we define Perceptual gain ratio as the SCOREQ increment per 10 − 3 10^{-3} reduction in SSL loss. The ratio substantially favors ERI, implying that SSL loss minimization more effectively leads to perceptual quality gain when equipped with ERI. Note that analyzing the perceptual correlation from Section 2.2 on a fully trained ERI is confounded, as at convergence both w/ ERI and w/o ERI learn to cleanse SSL features. The perceptual gain ratio instead directly measures whether ERI translates the SSL objective to perceptual quality in training. Design study Table 3 shows the design choice study results to measure the component-wise contribution in the proposed method. Modifying the ERI layer from 2 to 1 degrades perceptual quality, suggesting that injecting more restored features into the SSL backbone improves performance. Removing the sg on the SSL condition fusion degrades perceptual quality, attributable to the ineffective SSL loss minimization discussed in Section 3 . Lastly, changing the ERI mechanism from simple concatenation (i.e., default design) to more complicated AdaLN did not result in a significant performance gain, implying that ERI’s benefit comes from the intermediate-layer features themselves rather than the increased capacity. 6 Conclusions We discover perceptual correlation collapse: under severe degradation, the SSL feature cleansing objective does not fully align with the restoration objective. Though our correlation analysis relies on neural quality proxies for human perception, the agreement we observe across multiple proxies shows the trend is not an artifact of a single metric. To address perceptual correlation collapse, we propose Early Restoration Injection (ERI), which conditions SSL feature cleansing on intermediate features from the restoration model, supplying the SSL with partially restored evidence in place of severely degraded input. ERI adds only simple operations, and our experiments attribute its gain to the injected features themselves rather than to added capacity or a more expressive fusion mechanism.
